source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2
notes_on_source: Verse 26 is missing from the source (jumps from v25 to v27).

verses.translation: And as he drew near{H5066} to Yerushalayim{H3389}, at the Mount{H2022} of Olives{H2132}, he sent{H7971} two{H8147} disciples.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'at the Mount of Olives' only. Greek: 'to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives' (πρὸς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν πρὸς τὸ ὄρος τῶν ἐλαιῶν). Hebrew omits Bethphage and Bethany.
textual_notes: Zechariah 14:4: 'On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives.' The Hebrew preserves the Zechariah eschatological connection.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: Go{H1980} to that tower{H4026} that is before you, and as soon as you enter{H935} the midst{H8432}, you shall find{H4672} one{H259} colt{H5895} tied{H7194}, upon which no rider{H7392} has sat. Untie{H5425} it and bring{H935} it to me.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגדול (migdol — 'tower', H4026) where Greek has κώμην ('village'). A back-translator from 'village' would use כפר (kfar) or עיר (ir — 'town'). The Hebrew calls the destination a 'tower' — possibly a watchtower settlement or fortified village. The word מגדל is used for the Tower of Babel (Gen 11:4), the tower in the vineyard (Isa 5:2), and watchtowers (2 Kings 9:17, 17:9).

Uses עיר (ayir — 'colt/young donkey', H5895). This is the specific OT word from Zechariah 9:9: 'humble and riding upon a donkey, upon a colt (עיר) the foal of a she-donkey.' Greek has πῶλον ('colt'). While both mean 'colt,' the Hebrew uses the exact Zechariah prophecy word. A back-translator could use several words for 'colt'; the Hebrew author specifically chose the prophetic term.
textual_notes: Zechariah 9:9: 'Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion... your king comes to you, righteous and saved, humble and riding upon a donkey, upon a colt (עיר) the foal of a she-donkey.'

verses.translation: And if any man{H120} says{H559} to you: Why are you doing{H6213} this? — say{H559} that the Lord{H113} needs{H6878} him, and immediately they will let him go{H5117}.
And they went{H1980} and found{H4672} the colt{H5895} tied{H7194} before the door{H1817}, and they untied{H5425} it.
And those who were there said{H559} to them: Why are you untying{H5425} the colt{H5895}? What are you doing{H6213}?
And they said{H559} what Yeshua commanded{H6680} them.
And they let them bring{H1980} the colt{H5895} to Yeshua, and the disciples laid{H5117} their garments{H4403} upon it, and he rode{H7392}.
And many{H7227} men{H376} spread{H6584} their garments{H899} on the road{H1870}, and other{H312} peoples{H5971} cut{H3772} branches{H6057} from the trees{H6086} and covered the road{H1870}.

And those who walk{H1980} before him and those who follow{H4900} after him call out{H7121} and say{H559}: Save{H3467} us, O Savior{H3467}! Blessed{H1288}, blessed{H1288} is he who comes{H935} in the Name{H8034} of HaShem{H8034}!

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הושיענו מושיע (hoshi'enu moshia — 'save us, O Savior!'). Greek has ὡσαννά ('Hosanna'). The Greek merely transliterates the Hebrew הושע נא (hosha na — 'save, please'). But the Hebrew text UNPACKS it: 'save us' (הושיענו) + 'O Savior' (מושיע) — making the cry both a prayer AND a title. The crowd calls him מושיע (Moshia — 'Savior'). A back-translator from the Greek transliteration ὡσαννά would write הושענא — the transliterated form — NOT the expanded 'save us, O Savior.' The Hebrew gives the FULL liturgical meaning.
Double ברוך ברוך (barukh barukh — 'blessed, blessed') — emphatic doubling not in Greek, which has only one ὡσαννά followed by εὐλογημένος. The doubling is a Hebrew intensification device.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Save us, O Savior!' (הושיענו מושיע — prayer + title). Greek: 'Hosanna!' (ὡσαννά — transliterated exclamation). Hebrew unpacks the meaning; Greek preserves the sound.
Hebrew doubles 'blessed, blessed.' Greek has single 'blessed.'
translation_notes: Psalm 118:25-26 is the source: 'Save us, please (הושיעה נא), YHWH! ... Blessed is the one who comes in the Name of YHWH.' The Hebrew preserves the psalmic prayer.

verses.translation: And blessed{H1288} shall be the King{H4428}, the Savior{H3467}, from the heavens{H8064}!

one_way_hebrew: Uses המלך מושיע משמים (ha-melekh moshia mi-shamayim — 'the King, the Savior, from the heavens'). Greek has ἡ ἐρχομένη βασιλεία τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Δαυΐδ ('the coming kingdom of our father David'). Completely different proclamations: Hebrew acclaims a PERSON (the King-Savior from heaven); Greek acclaims a THING (the coming kingdom of David). A back-translator would never convert 'the coming kingdom of our father David' into 'the King, the Savior, from heaven.'
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'blessed is the King, the Savior, from heaven' (a person). Greek: 'blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David' (a system). Entirely different objects of blessing.

verses.translation: And they entered{H935} Yerushalayim{H3389}, into the Temple{H4720}, and he looked at{H5027} all{H3605} that was inside{H6441}. And in the evening{H6153} he went out{H3318} to Beit Aniyah with the twelve{H8147}{H6240} disciples.

translation_notes: בית עניה (Beit Aniyah — 'House of Poverty/Affliction'). The Hebrew place name is meaningful: the King-Savior lodges in the 'House of Affliction.'

verses.translation: And the next day{H3117} he went out{H3318} from Beit Aniyah, and he had a great{H1419} hunger{H7458}.

And when from afar{H7350} he saw{H7200} a fig tree{H8384} bearing leaves{H5929}, he went{H1980} to see{H7200} if he might find{H4672} figs{H8384}. And when he came{H935} to it, he found{H4672} nothing but leaves{H5929}, for it was not the season{H6256} of figs{H8384}.

textual_notes: The fig tree as a symbol of Israel: Jeremiah 8:13 'I will surely consume them, says YHWH: no grapes on the vine, no figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall wither.' Hosea 9:10 'I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers like the first fruit on the fig tree.' The fig tree's failure to produce fruit despite showing leaves symbolizes Israel's outward piety without inner fruit.

verses.translation: And Yeshua answered{H6030}, saying{H559} to it: From now{H6258} and onward I wish{H7521} that no one{H259} shall eat{H398} fruit{H6529} from you. And this his disciples heard{H8085}.

And they came{H935} to Yerushalayim{H3389}. And when he entered{H935} the Temple{H4720}, he began to drive out{H1644} the sellers{H4376} and the buyers{H7069} in the Temple{H4720}; and the purchases of the money-changers and the tables{H7979} of those who sell{H4376} the doves{H3123} he overturned{H2015}, from top to bottom.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גירש (gerash — 'drove out/expelled', H1644). This is the verb God uses when expelling Adam from Eden (Gen 3:24: ויגרש את האדם — 'and he drove out the man') and when Israel drove out the Canaanites (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27, Josh 24:12,18). Greek has ἤρξατο ἐκβάλλειν ('began to cast out'). The Hebrew frames the Temple cleansing as an EXPULSION — the same act as the expulsion from Eden and the expulsion of the nations.

verses.translation: And he did not allow{H5800} anyone to carry{H5375} any burden{H4853} through the Temple{H4720}.

And he taught{H3925} them and said{H559} to them: Is it not written{H3789} that my house{H1004} is a house of prayer{H8605} for all{H3605} the peoples{H5971}? And you have made{H6213} it a den{H4631} of robbers{H1590}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM OT QUOTATIONS: (1) Isaiah 56:7 — בית תפלה לכל העמים ('a house of prayer for all the peoples'). The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact wording. (2) Jeremiah 7:11 — מערת גנבים (me'arat gannavim — 'a den of robbers'). Both prophetic quotations are preserved in their original Hebrew form. A back-translator from Greek would produce similar text, but the Hebrew IS the source text of both prophecies.
textual_notes: Isaiah 56:7: 'For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.' Jeremiah 7:11: 'Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?'

verses.translation: And when the chief{H8269} priests{H3548} heard{H8085} it, and the wise-men of the signs, they sought{H1245} how they might kill{H4191} him; but they feared{H3372} him, for all{H3605} the people{H5971} were astonished{H8539} at his teachings.
And when evening{H6153} came, he went out{H3318} from the city{H5892}.
In the morning{H1242}, when they passed{H5674} the fig tree{H8384}, they saw{H7200} that it had withered{H3001} to the root{H8328}.
And then Keyfa remembered{H2142} and said{H559} to him: Rabbi, behold{H2009}! The fig tree{H8384} that you cursed{H7043} has withered{H3001}.
And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559} to him: Let there be good{H2896} faith{H530} in HaShem{H8034}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Let there be good faith in HaShem.' Greek: ἔχετε πίστιν θεοῦ ('Have faith of/in God'). The Hebrew adds טובה ('good') — qualifying the faith.

verses.translation: For truly{H571} I say{H559} to you: Whoever says{H559} to one{H259} mountain{H2022} 'Arise{H6965} and enter{H935} the sea{H3220}!' and does not doubt{H6601} in his heart{H3820} — immediately it shall be done{H6213}.
And for the sake of your love{H160} I say{H559}: In all{H3605} your prayers{H8605}, let there be strong{H2389} faith{H530} in God{H410}, and you shall obtain{H5381} all{H3605} that you ask{H7592}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אהבתכם (ahavatkhem — 'your love', H160). Greek has no equivalent phrasing — it simply says 'whatever you ask in prayer.' The Hebrew frames the teaching as motivated by love for the disciples.

verses.translation: And when you stand{H5975} in prayer{H8605}, forgive{H4229} if you have any complaint{H8519} against any man{H120}, so that your Father{H1} in heaven{H8064} may forgive{H4229} your iniquities{H5771}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עונותיכם (avonoteikhem — 'your iniquities', H5771). Greek has τὰ παραπτώματα ὑμῶν ('your trespasses'). Hebrew עון (avon — 'iniquity') is heavier than Greek παράπτωμα ('trespass/misstep'). Avon implies deep moral twisting/perversion (Gen 4:13, 15:16, Ps 32:5, 51:4, Isa 53:5,6); trespass implies stepping over a boundary. A back-translator from 'trespass' would use פשע (pesha — 'transgression'), not the deeper עון.

Uses תרעומת (tar'omet — 'complaint/grievance', H8519). Greek has εἴ τι ἔχετε κατά τινος ('if you have anything against anyone'). The Hebrew uses a specific noun for the grievance; the Greek uses a general construction.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your iniquities' (עונות — deep moral failings). Greek: 'your trespasses' (παραπτώματα — boundary violations). Different severity.

verses.translation: And immediately they entered{H935} Yerushalayim{H3389}. And when he went{H1980} in the Temple{H4720}, the chief{H8269} priests{H3548} and the wise-men of the signs and the elders{H2205} drew near{H7126} to him.
And they said{H559} to him: By what power{H3581} do you do{H6213} these wonders{H6381}? And who gave{H5414} you this power{H3581} that you do{H6213} this?

one_way_hebrew: Uses נפלאות (nifla'ot — 'wonders', H6381) — the OT word for God's miraculous acts. Greek has ταῦτα ('these things'). The Hebrew specifies 'wonders'; the Greek says merely 'things.' The Hebrew frames the question in terms of divine wonder-working authority.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'these wonders' (נפלאות — miraculous acts). Greek: 'these things' (ταῦτα — generic). Hebrew is more specific.

verses.translation: And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559} to them: I shall ask{H7592} you one{H259} thing{H1697} — answer{H6030} me, and afterward I shall say{H559} to you by what power{H3581} I do{H6213} these things.
The immersion{H2881} of Yochanan{H3110} — was it from the heavens{H8064} or from men{H376}? Answer{H6030} me.
And they thought{H2803} among themselves: If we say{H559} 'from the heavens{H8064},' he will say{H559} to us: 'If so, why do you not believe{H539}?'
And if we say{H559} 'from men{H376}' — they feared{H3372} the people{H5971}, for all{H3605} of them held{H6965} in truth{H571} that Yochanan{H3110} was a prophet{H5030}.
And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559} to them: And I shall not say{H559} to you by what power I do{H6213} these things.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 11 in Hebrew centers on the Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing. The strongest one-way markers are: (1) הושיענו מושיע ('Save us, O Savior!', v9) where Greek has the transliterated ὡσαννά — the Hebrew UNPACKS the Hosanna, making it both a prayer and a messianic title. No back-translator from the Greek transliteration would produce this expanded form. (2) המלך מושיע משמים ('the King, the Savior, from heaven', v10) vs. Greek's 'the coming kingdom of our father David' — completely different proclamations (a person vs. a system). (3) מגדול ('tower', v2) vs. Greek 'village' — a different place designation. (4) עיר (ayir — 'colt', v2) — the specific Zechariah 9:9 word for the donkey of the messianic entry. (5) גירש ('drove out/expelled', v15) — the Eden-expulsion verb applied to the Temple cleansing, framing it as a divine expulsion like Genesis 3:24. (6) עונותיכם ('your iniquities', v25) vs. Greek 'trespasses' — a heavier moral category. The chapter preserves both OT quotations (Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11) in their original Hebrew form.
